g1_rf2#1.killer: delivered system $ per GB of SRAM, which depends on how many MB fit on a ~100 mm² N6 die
g1_rf2#1.why: The economics are sound if built at cost, but the claim relies on SRAM density about 25% above any shipped pure-SRAM die, and a vendor markup would push it past the $1.5k/GB limit.

baseline_1#4.killer: peak temperature of DRAM stacked on a roughly 2 kW logic die. The idea's own gate is DRAM ≤95 °C.
baseline_1#4.why: The parts that work are what incumbents already do, and the one new part, logic-on-DRAM at 2 kW, fails its own 95 °C gate by about 2x in rise above coolant.

g1_mech#1.killer: quality loss at about 2 bits per weight. The idea's stated deciding quantity was decode energy; I chose quality instead because it fails first at the scale the idea needs.
g1_mech#1.why: At 2 bits per weight, quality falls about 10x below what production serving accepts. Measured against FP4 rather than FP8, the gain is under 1.5x. QTIP's own computed codes already regenerate the codebook without storing a table.

baseline_2#1.killer: SRAM capacity per package for pinning 545 GB of weights in a 144-package domain
baseline_2#1.why: The bandwidth split is a sound idea, but SRAM density is about 2x short. That breaks the 144-package fit and leaves at most 1.2x net cost gain.

g1_mech#2.killer: KV compression versus FP16 reached at ≤1% accuracy loss at 128K context
g1_mech#2.why: It is physically fine, but it buys only 1.7× on KV over NVFP4, which is about 1.12–1.17× on the whole system, and its accuracy at 128K has never been measured.

baseline_2#2.killer: heat from about 10 PF FP8 of logic in the HBM4 base dies, which sit under the DRAM
baseline_2#2.why: The 3.7× comes from the sparse model, which incumbents also run. The near-HBM engine is sized for dense intensity (450 FLOP/B) and cannot be cooled under DRAM, and with the bandwidth unchanged it barely changes $/Mtok.

baseline_1#1.killer: hybrid-bonded DRAM capacity per package at 64 TB/s, which needs 0.20 Gb/mm² per DRAM die and 50 GB/s/Gb
baseline_1#1.why: The roofline gain is real, about 2.3× per kW and about 2.6× per package. But it depends on 160 GB of hybrid-bonded DRAM per package, about 2× what is claimed as mature, and on a full-access energy no one has measured. Delivering about 2.7 kA up through the DRAM stack to the logic is also an open problem.

baseline_2#4.killer: C-SKU training throughput per package compared with Rubin
baseline_2#4.why: A product-line choice that gives at most about 5–7% on prefill and loses or ties on training is not a lead.

g1_rf2#2.killer: SRAM left for KV cache after the weights, measured as concurrent users at 500 tok/s on 8k-in/1k-out traffic (~9k-token context; MiniMax-M2 has 62 layers × 8 KV heads × head dim 128, so KV is 127 KB/token at FP8 and 71 KB at NVFP4). To get near GB300's $/Mtok, a 3-wafer system at ~$571/hr TCO (3 × ~$3M CS-3-class wafers over 4 years, with the package taken as 45% of TCO) has to sell ~2.64M tok/s
g1_rf2#2.why: Keeping all 230B parameters in SRAM leaves almost no room for KV cache, so the batch is roughly 20–90× too small to amortise wafer-class silicon; also, 300 GB in "2.5–3 wafers" needs ~100–120 GB per wafer, against WSE-3's 44 GB (≈6.8 wafers at WSE-3 density).

baseline_1#3.killer: Decode power per package at Rubin-class 22 TB/s. "2× tokens per kW" needs ≤ half of Rubin's decode draw (taken as 0.8 × ~2.3 kW TDP, an analyst estimate). The floor is HBM read at 3.44–5.74 pJ/bit, plus 3.6 TB/s scale-up SerDes at ~5 pJ/bit, plus on-die movement at ~1 pJ/bit, plus ~100 W for compute and leakage
baseline_1#3.why: The trade-offs are stated honestly and the design is physically plausible, but HBM access energy alone takes most of the claimed 2× power budget, and energy is only ~9% of TCO, so even a full 2× tok/kW cuts cost per token by about 1.1–1.3×, short of 1.5×.

cross_g1#1.killer: Bandwidth per user while layers are pipelined. Each pipeline stage can only read its own bits, so the 42 TB/s total equals per-user bandwidth only if every chiplet works on every layer. "Package links" means at least 2 stages. At the measured 0.064 Gb/mm², 312 Gb needs 4,875 mm², or 1.5 packages of 3,200 mm².
cross_g1#1.why: Stacked eDRAM is cheap, but the 1,000 tok/s/user claim treats total bandwidth as per-user bandwidth, which layer pipelining does not give, so it delivers about 500 tok/s/user unless all chiplets are tensor-parallel on every layer.

cross_g1#2.killer: DRAM areal density for 80 GB on 2 chiplets × 4 layers. Chiplet area is not stated; I took about 400 mm² from the sibling design.
cross_g1#2.why: It needs the same 0.20 Gb/mm² "no room left" density that idea 3 had to drop, which is ~3× the measured hybrid-bonded density. Its current claim is also internally off by 2×: 1 kW at 0.75 V across 2 stacks is ~667 A per stack, not 340 A.

improve_g1#2.killer: Wide-I/O hybrid-bonded DRAM areal density per layer
improve_g1#2.why: The physics adds up (DRAM power 450 W checks out, and bandwidth per bit is under the measured 135 GB/s/Gb), but the one deciding density has only been shown at 64% of what is needed. Heat from the logic die on DRAM is a second open risk, since imec's 3D layout reached 141.7 °C without mitigations.

improve_g1#1.killer: Per-user speed when SRAM-resident weights are pipelined layer by layer. Only the dies that hold layer ℓ can compute it, so a token's time per step is L·F/P_total. My script reproduces the idea's own 62.8 GB and 5.0 PF as a known-answer check.
improve_g1#1.why: The density, capacity and compute totals check out, but layer-serial pipelining limits it to about half of the claimed 1,000 tok/s/user. Its $0.068 claim also rests on full pipeline utilisation that 31 users across 80 stages cannot provide, and it leaves out facility and network costs.

cross_g1#3.killer: how much of each Rubin package's HBM time per decode step goes to reading weights, at ≥300 tok/s/user, with the 545 GB of weights spread across all 72 NVL72 packages. Moving weights into SRAM can only free that share.
cross_g1#3.why: Decode is bound by bandwidth, not capacity, so the extra HBM pool adds no users. Freeing the ~10% weight share is worth at most ~1.1×, and the base-die premium cancels that.

improve_g1#3.killer: the same weight-read share of Rubin's HBM time per decode step at 300 tok/s/user. The claimed per-MW gain of 1.41× at 8K needs that share to be 1 − 1/1.41.
improve_g1#3.why: The claimed gain needs about 3× more weight traffic per step than a fully sharded Rubin actually has, so the real net is about 1.0×. The 128K claim also runs the wrong way. The idea only survives if Rubin can't reach 300 tok/s/user at all because of latency overheads, which is a separate claim the idea does not make or test.

improve_g2#2.killer: DRAM bandwidth per Gb at 64 Mb/mm², 4 layers (48.9 GB of capacity must deliver 44 TB/s)
improve_g2#2.why: The numbers hold by my roofline, but the margin is only 1.2. It rests on one trade-press bandwidth figure paired with a density from a different chip, and the 4-layer stack at 64 Mb/mm² has not been built, so this is fragile.

cross_g2#3.killer: The package cost needed for a 1.5× cut in cost per token over the whole TCO, using ledger A shares (package 45%, everything else unchanged)
cross_g2#3.why: It works only by avoiding a vendor's margin. Against TPU-style in-house silicon the gain falls to about 1.15×, and the claimed 2.7× is an accounting error.

improve_g2#1.killer: All-reduce latency across 32 dies on an organic package, with about 9.4 all-reduces per stage
improve_g2#1.why: The cost win holds even if per-user speed falls to Groq levels. It is still 2–4× more expensive per token than GB300 at 50 tok/s and slower than Cerebras, as the idea itself says.

cross_g2#1.killer: Per-user decode rate when each layer is pipelined die by die: one token must read 39.7 GB of NVFP4 weights in sequence at 0.864 TB/s per die
cross_g2#1.why: Higher storage density does not fix sequential bandwidth. Die-by-die pipelining gives about 22 tok/s/user, slower than a single GPU, and costs about 4× more per token.

improve_g2#3.killer: Cut in package price that a 192 GB, 5 PF, 1.2 TB/s part gets against a $55k Rubin. The 22 TB/s stays, so decode tok/s per package is unchanged and every gain must come from cost.
improve_g2#3.why: The physics holds (2.4× capacity headroom, and the bandwidth is unchanged), but the gain is capped below 1.5× by its own numbers. Whether it even reaches 1.2× depends on Nvidia or an ASIC vendor passing the BOM savings into the price, which no engineering choice controls.

cross_g2#2.why: Its own claim to depend "only on measured" data fails. The one measured hybrid-bond chip delivers about 7.5× less bandwidth per mm² than the design assumes. Even at the assumed bandwidth, 25.6 GB per package is too small to batch enough users to spread the cost of reading the weights, so it loses about 5× on tokens per kW to Rubin.
